how: A digital wedding invitation on InvitesReady is one link, not a PDF and not a stack of printed cards. You pick an animated design, add the names and the schedule in the browser, and send that link on WhatsApp. Guests open it on their phone and reply on the page. They do not install an app.

Start on the wedding page or the template gallery. Open a design and watch the seal, the door, or the gate before you type anything. Lotus Lens is a courtyard save-the-date. Vivah opens like temple doors onto the muhurtham. Gazal carries a nikah and a walima. Thiruvizha can be read in English, Tamil, or both. The same steps work for a birthday, a baptism, or a housewarming.

Personalising happens in the browser. You add the hosts, the couple or the person being celebrated, each function with its time and place, a map, photographs, and the line you want guests to read. A wedding can list the ceremony, the reception, and the gatherings around them on one page. If a muhurat or a venue changes after the link is already in the family group, you edit the page and the same link updates. You do not send a second card.

Sharing is a copy and paste. Put the link in a WhatsApp chat or a group. Guests tap it, the invitation opens in the phone's browser, and the reply stays on that page. You can see who is coming, including a reply per function when the design asks for one. Wishes sit with the reply. The address can stay off the page, or appear after someone says yes.

Some wedding designs are free to publish, including Gazal. Others list their own one-time price on the template page. Vivah is ₹379. There is not one from-price that covers every design. Publishing is free for now while those prices are paused. When you are ready, browse the templates or read the questions about RSVP, editing, and WhatsApp.
features: A digital invitation from InvitesReady is a page your guests open from one link. The opening is animated: a seal breaks, doors part, a veil lifts, or a letter tears. After that they see the names, the schedule, and a place to reply. Nothing is installed, and they do not create an account.

The schedule is part of the invitation. A wedding page can hold the muhurtham, a haldi, a mehendi, a sangeet, and the reception, each with its own time, place, and dress note. A birthday, baptism, or housewarming uses the same idea for a single gathering. The venue can include a map. You choose how much of the address to show before a guest has said yes, and a page can be protected with a password.

Photographs and music depend on the design. Where the template has a gallery or a track, you upload them in the browser and guests see or hear them on the page. Wishes and duas sit with the reply, so you are not collecting notes in a dozen chats. Replies stay on your invitation. Guests do not see other people's answers, and you can review the list from your account.

The link does not change when the details do. Edit a time, a venue, or a name after you have shared it, and the next open shows the new version. That matters for a muhurat that moves, or a venue that is confirmed late. You can still send a short WhatsApp note, but you do not attach a new PDF.

Languages follow the design and the wording you type. Most templates are set in English, and the lines themselves can be written in the language your families use. Thiruvizha can show the page in English, Tamil, or both. Prices are listed on each template. Gazal is free to publish. Vivah is ₹379, paid once, and other designs differ. Publishing is free for now while prices are paused.
guides: These guides are for people writing an Indian wedding invitation, or deciding whether the card should be digital. Each article will hold wording you can adapt, plus the practical piece that usually gets left off the card: how to send it, what it costs, and how replies come back.

The Hindu wedding wording guide will show how parents and the couple are named, a line for the muhurtham, and short lines for haldi, mehendi, sangeet, and the reception. The nikah guide will cover the families, the nikah, the walima, and a request for duas. The Tamil guide will give the same invitation in English and in Tamil, and say when to show both on one card. Those three link to the Hindu wedding, nikah, and Tamil wedding pages, and to Vivah, Gazal, and Thiruvizha.

The WhatsApp guide will be the message you paste above the link: one for a family group, one for a single guest, and what to say when a date changes but the link stays the same. The cost guide will compare a printed card, priced per guest, with a digital card paid once. The RSVP guide will walk through one link for several functions, what the guest sees when they reply, and how to take the guest list with you.

The articles below are outlines, marked to be written, and they are not indexed yet. The pages they point at are live: digital wedding invitations, the occasion pages, and the template for each tradition. If you only need the card, start with the wedding invitations rather than waiting on a guide.
